Some of my struggle with the scope of the work may be in how it's framed in the introduction. The intro discusses the open question of how the brain represents similarities in objects, but then that question is never answered. It's also not clear to me what the key novelty is of the study beyond prior work, and how that changes our understanding of the human visual system. I'm also not sure why real-world objects are an interesting set or novelty (versus other types of stimuli we'd expect to have more idiosyncratic representations).

I also have the question of whether the offline object arrangement task could have influenced the similarity structure reflected in the brain.

Also, most of the analyses looked at correlations between individuals' brain and behavior to look at "perceived visual similarity". However, the behavioral measure includes both what we can consider the group-shared visual similarity (the mean, perhaps even capturing the "objective visual similarity"), and the individual-specific visual similarity (the variance). I am curious to see what regions still show a correlation with behavior even if you remove the mean -- so, for example, if you calculate an RDM factoring out / partial out the group mean, is it the PRC and alErC that show a correlation with really this individual-specific RDM? That being said, your later analysis showing higher correlations with an individual's behavioral RDM than other participants' RDMs answers this question in a different way. But the method I suggest also isolates the representation specific to the individual.

With that, I wonder if one can begin to look at the causes of these idiosyncracies. Since the current study is looking at visual similarity, I kept wondering if it would make sense to get an "objective" measure of visual similarity, by creating RDMs formed from some sort of computer vision metric (e.g., pixel similarity, or a DNN metric). You could examine the degree to which individuals agree / disagree with objective similarity, and how that relates to patterns in the brain. I wouldn't say this is necessary, but one potential direction that could expand the impact of the current work.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors argue in the Discussion for a modest relationship between perceived and objective measures of similarity (p23), and as such "the coding of whole objects based on complex feature conjunctions in PrC and alErC could afford the flexibility that is required to capture these differences in perception". What does "complex" mean here? Specifically, it is unclear as to whether the authors are suggesting that "subjectively perceived aspects" of stimuli constitute just another set of features (in addition to objective perceptual/semantic features), or something else entirely.

One inference the paper makes is that all 10 items contribute to the PRC/ERC effects equally. Do the authors have any evidence for this? How similar were the 10 different item categories? More specifically, did they have similar between-exemplar similarity ratings? This could maybe be inferred maybe from SFig1B for 5 of the items.

Absent from much of the framing in this paper is the characterization of perceptual verses semantic similarity, in favor of a coarse/fine-grained motif. However, some of these elements may be influencing the Supplementary analysis of centroid similarity. For example, in the first stage of the iMDS when all 10 categories of items are on the screen, it's unlikely that raters can do a purely visual decomposition of the visual similarity, despite the instructions. As such, there may be some "semantic similarity" in these groupings (and the consequent centroids). Could the authors speak to whether their Supplementary analyses of these relationships (SFig4) address this semantic factor?

Do the authors see any similarities in their LOC result for SFig4B, and the ITC-centered results in Charest et al., 2014? Some mention of this in the Discussion paragraph might help to draw further links between these papers.

claims.claim: Vision neuroscience has made great strides in understanding the hierarchical organization of object representations along the ventral visual stream (VVS).
claims.source: Vision neuroscience has made great strides in understanding the hierarchical organization of object representations along the ventral visual stream (VVS).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the field of vision neuroscience that draws from established scientific consensus.

claims.claim: Activity patterns in PrC and alErC predict the structure of perceived visual similarity relationships among category exemplars with higher precision than any other VVS region.
claims.source: As anticipated, we found that activity patterns in PrC and alErC predicted the structure of perceived visual similarity relationships among category exemplars, including its observer-specific component, with higher precision than any other VVS region.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI data and representational similarity analyses presented in the study, as shown in Figures 3-7.

claims.claim: Perceived visual similarities are important for categorizing a fruit at the grocery store as an apple rather than a pear.
claims.source: Perceived similarities are important, for example, for categorizing a fruit at the grocery store as an apple rather than a pear.
claims.evidence: This is an illustrative example drawing from common knowledge about everyday perceptual tasks.

claims.claim: The similarity of objects influences performance in numerous behavioural contexts, including but not limited to categorization, object discrimination, recognition memory, and prediction.
claims.source: Indeed, experimental work in psychology has confirmed that the similarity of objects influences performance in numerous behavioural contexts, including but not limited to categorization, object discrimination, recognition memory, and prediction (see Medin et al., 1993; Goldstone and Son, 2012; Hebart et al., 2020, for review).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research reviews.

claims.claim: Activity patterns in a large expanse of the ventral visual stream capture much of the category structure in the environment.
claims.source: Findings from this research indicate that activity patterns in a large expanse of the ventral visual stream (VVS), often referred to as inferotemporal (IT) cortex or ventral temporal cortex, capture much of this structure in the environment (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Connolly et al., 2012; Mur et al., 2013; Proklova et al., 2016; Cichy et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI studies.

claims.claim: Numerous studies have revealed a similarity-based clustering of response patterns for objects in IT that is tied to category membership.
claims.source: For example, numerous studies have revealed a similarity-based clustering of response patterns for objects in IT that is tied to category membership (e.g., Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Proklova et al., 2016; see Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014 for review).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claims.claim: The representational–hierarchical model of object processing in the VVS asserts that structures in the medial temporal lobe constitute the apex of its processing hierarchy.
claims.source: The representational–hierarchical model of object processing in the VVS asserts that structures in the medial temporal lobe constitute the apex of its processing hierarchy (Murray and Bussey, 1999; Bussey and Saksida, 2007; Cowell et al., 2010; Kent et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical papers proposing the representational-hierarchical model.

claims.claim: Visual objects are thought to be represented in PrC in their most highly integrated form based on complex feature conjunctions.
claims.source: Visual objects are thought to be represented in PrC in their most highly integrated form based on complex feature conjunctions (Murray and Bussey, 1999; Buckley and Gaffan, 2006; Bussey and Saksida, 2007; Graham et al., 2010; Kent et al., 2016), which support perceptual discrimination of even highly similar exemplars from the same object category (e.g., O'Neil et al., 2013; O'Neil et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical papers on PrC function.

claims.claim: Lateral entorhinal cortex has been suggested to extend the role of PrC in visual object discrimination through integration with additional spatial features.
claims.source: Lateral entorhinal cortex (or its human homologue anterolateral entorhinal cortex [alErC; Maass et al., 2015; Yeung et al., 2017]) has been suggested to extend this role in visual object discrimination through integration with additional spatial features (Connor and Knierim, 2017; Yeung et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on entorhinal cortex function.

claims.claim: Patients with medial temporal lobe lesions that include PrC and alErC show deficits in oddity-discrimination tasks when complex objects with substantial feature overlap are compared.
claims.source: A finding documented in multiple reports (Buckley et al., 2001; Barense et al., 2007; Bartko et al., 2007; Inhoff et al., 2019; cf., Stark and Squire, 2000; Levy et al., 2005; Hales and Clark, 2015) is that patients with medial temporal lobe lesions that include PrC and alErC show deficits in oddity-discrimination tasks when complex objects with substantial feature overlap are compared, but not when oddity judgements require comparison of simple visual stimuli that can be distinguished based on a single feature such as colour or luminance.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple lesion studies.

claims.claim: Discrimination performance during scanning was highly sensitive to perceived visual similarities among exemplars.
claims.source: At the behavioural level, we found that discrimination performance was highly sensitive to fine-grained perceived similarity among exemplars, including those aspects that were observer specific.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict fine-grained structure within categories with higher precision than any other VVS region.
claims.source: Representational similarity analyses (RSAs) of ultra-high-resolution fMRI data revealed, in line with our hypotheses, that activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict this fine-grained structure within categories with higher precision than any other VVS region, and that they predict even those aspects of similarity structure that are unique to individual observers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results presented in Figures 3-7.

claims.claim: The mean intersubject correlation for perceived similarity ratings across all exemplars and categories was r = 0.69.
claims.source: Examination of intersubject correlations of each participant's RDM and the mean of all other participants' RDMs (excluding their own) revealed a mean value of r = 0.69 (t-test r > 0: p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the iMDS task.

claims.claim: Average ratings of perceived similarity correlate with estimates from the HMAX model (r = 0.25, p < 0.001).
claims.source: When we calculated an RDM for ratings averaged across participants, and compared it with an RDM derived from a computational model developed to capture objects at their intermediate visual feature level (HMAX, Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Cadieu et al., 2007; Serre et al., 2007; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014), we also found a significant correlation (r = 0.25, p < 0.001), suggesting that average ratings capture a shared component in the subjective ratings that relate to objective image characteristics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral ratings and HMAX model estimates.

claims.claim: HMAX model estimates were only significantly correlated with average ratings at low and medium levels of similarity, but not at high levels.
claims.source: Follow-up analyses that focussed on this relationship in different subranges of similarity among exemplars (low, medium, and high; see Figure 1B) revealed, however, that the estimates derived from the HMAX model were only significantly correlated with average ratings at low and medium levels (low r = 0.45; p < 0.001; medium r = 0.24; p < 0.001; high r = 0.05; p > 0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific correlation analyses between behavioral ratings and HMAX estimates.

claims.claim: At their finest grain, judgements of similarity within categories rely on integrated object representations that are not captured by intermediate feature-level descriptions and are observer specific.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that at their finest grain, judgements of similarity within categories rely on integrated object representations that (1) are not captured by intermediate feature-level descriptions, and (2) are observer specific.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of correlations between HMAX estimates and behavioral ratings at different levels of similarity.

claims.claim: Individual differences in perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars are temporally stable observer characteristics.
claims.source: Critically, in a separate behavioural experiment conducted in another sample of participants with multiple assessments, we found that individual differences in perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars are temporally stable observer characteristics (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by test-retest data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Response errors on same category trials increased with increasing visual similarity.
claims.source: Specifically, response errors on same category trials increased with increasing visual similarity (significant linear slope; t(22) = 18.35, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Response times for correct responses on same category trials were positively correlated with perceived visual similarity level.
claims.source: Moreover, response times for correct responses on same category trials were positively correlated with perceived visual similarity level (t(22) = 13.47, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Task performance was more sensitive to participants' own similarity ratings than to other participants' ratings.
claims.source: When we compared the influence of participant's own similarity ratings with that of others on behaviour (Figure 2B,C), we found a significantly larger positive slope in error rate (t(22) = 8.30; p < 0.0001) and in response times (t(22) = 9.68; p < 0.0001) for participants' own ratings.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral performance using own versus other participants' ratings.

claims.claim: Neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC correlated with participants' perceived visual similarity RDMs (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
claims.source: Our analyses revealed that neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC did indeed correlate with participants' perceived visual similarity RDMs (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Patterns in EVC and LOC were significantly correlated with behavior-based RDMs.
claims.source: Patterns in other regions of the VVS (EVC, p < 0.003; LOC, p < 0.002) were also significantly correlated with these behaviour-based RDMs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Patterns in PhC and pmErC did not predict the perceived similarity structure for objects.
claims.source: Critically, patterns in regions previously implicated in scene processing, specifically PhC and pmErC (Schultz et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015; Schröder et al., 2015), did not predict the perceived similarity structure for objects (all p > 0.5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D and citations to prior research on these regions.

claims.claim: Correlations between perceived similarity structure and activity patterns in PrC and alErC were significant at all three levels of similarity (low, medium, and high).
claims.source: Correlations between perceived similarity structure and activity patterns in PrC and alErC were significant at all three levels of similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific RSA results shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Correlations for activity patterns in posterior VVS regions (EVC and LOC) were significant only at the lowest level of perceived similarity.
claims.source: In contrast, correlations for activity patterns in posterior VVS regions were significant only at the lowest level of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific RSA results shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Correlations in PrC and alErC were higher than in LOC and EVC at medium and high levels of perceived similarity.
claims.source: Direct comparison between regions also revealed that correlations in PrC and alErC were higher than in LOC and EVC at medium and high levels of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by direct statistical comparisons of RSA results across regions shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Activity patterns associated with specific exemplars can be successfully classified in PrC and alErC at higher levels of perceived similarity than in posterior VVS regions.
claims.source: They confirmed that activity patterns associated with specific exemplars can indeed be successfully classified in PrC and alErC at higher levels of perceived similarity than in posterior VVS regions (Figure 4B for further detail).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: PrC and alErC were the only regions in the entire scanned brain volume whose patterns correlated with observer's reports when similarity between exemplars was perceived to be high.
claims.source: Critically, our searchlight analyses revealed that PrC and alErC were indeed the only regions in the entire scanned brain volume whose patterns correlated with observer's reports when similarity between exemplars was perceived to be high, and objects were most difficult to discriminate on the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 5E,F.

claims.claim: Activity patterns in EVC and LOC showed a significant correlation with the HMAX model at low and medium but not at the highest level of similarity.
claims.source: Activity patterns in EVC and LOC showed a significant correlation with the HMAX model at low and medium but not at the highest level of similarity; Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results comparing brain patterns to HMAX estimates shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Activity patterns in PrC and alErC did not correlate with estimates from the HMAX model nor with average ratings at any level of object similarity.
claims.source: Critically, activity patterns in PrC and alErC did not correlate with estimates from the HMAX model nor with average ratings at any level of object similarity (all Bonferroni-corrected p > 0.05; see Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: Activity patterns in VVS regions posterior to PrC and alErC capture the components of perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars that is shared by observers and closely related to object features at the intermediate feature level.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that activity in VVS regions posterior to PrC and alErC capture the components of perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars that is shared by observers and that is closely related to object features at the intermediate feature level.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of correlations between brain activity, average ratings, and HMAX estimates.

claims.claim: Neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict observer-specific perceived visual similarity structure.
claims.source: These analyses confirmed our expectation that the neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict observer-specific perceived visual similarity structure (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by i-index analyses shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Activation patterns in posterior VVS regions (EVC and LOC) did not uniquely predict participants' own perceived similarity structure.
claims.source: In contrast, activation patterns in posterior VVS regions, EVC and LOC (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] > 0.05) did not uniquely predict participants' own perceived similarity structure (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by i-index analyses shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: PrC and alErC showed significant brain–behaviour i-indices even when analyses were restricted to high levels of perceived similarity.
claims.source: Critically, PrC and alErC showed significant brain–behaviour i-indices even when we restricted analyses to fine-grained differentiation, that is, to the subrange of high levels of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific i-index analyses shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: A total of 29 participants completed the perceived similarity iMDS arrangement task and fMRI experiment.
claims.source: A total of 29 participants completed the perceived similarity iMDS arrangement task and fMRI experiment (12 females; age range = 18–35 years old; mean age = 24.2 years).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claims.claim: 23 participants were included in the final analyses after exclusions.
claims.source: Three participants were removed due to excessive head motion above the cutoff of 0.8 mm of framewise displacement, one participant weas removed due to behavioural performance accuracy 2 SD below the average on the fMRI task, and two participants were removed due to poor signal quality in medial temporal-lobe regions, i.e., a temporal signal-to-noise ratio 2 SD below average (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 Figure 1). Therefore, 23 participants were included in the final analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size after exclusions.

claims.claim: 40 greyscale images of objects from 10 categories were used as stimuli.
claims.source: We used 40 greyscale images of objects from 10 categories (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus set, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Each category was made up of four exemplars that all shared the same name.
claims.source: Each category in our set was made up of four exemplars that all shared the same name (e.g., apple, lipstick, and stapler).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus structure.

claims.claim: Participants completed eight functional runs that each lasted 4 minutes.
claims.source: Participants completed a total of eight functional runs that each lasted 4 min (stimulus duration = 1.2 s, intertrial interval = 1 s).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claims.claim: Each of the 40 exemplars were presented 3 times as no-response trials per run, for a total of 24 presentations on no-response trials across the entire experiment.
claims.source: Within each run, each of the 40 exemplars were presented 3 times as no-response trials, and once as a catch trial, for a total of 24 presentations on no-response trials and 8 catch trials (excluded from fMRI analyses) per exemplar across the entire experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claims.claim: MRI data were acquired using a 3T MR system with a 32-channel head coil.
claims.source: MRI data were acquired using a 3T MR system (Siemens). A 32-channel head coil was used.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the MRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: T2*-weighted data were collected at ultra-high resolution (1.7 × 1.7 mm) to optimize differentiation of BOLD signal in anterolateral versus posterior medial entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: T2*-weighted data were collected at this ultra-high resolution so as to optimize differentiation of BOLD signal in anterolateral versus posterior medial entorhinal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for the imaging resolution.

claims.claim: Automated segmentation was employed to delineate PrC, ErC, and PhC using ASHS.
claims.source: Automated segmentation was employed to delineate PrC, ErC, and PhC (ASHS; Wisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROI definition method with citation.

claims.claim: Each ERC was manually segmented into alErC and pmErC following a protocol developed by Yeung et al., 2017.
claims.source: We manually segmented each ERC obtained from ASHS into alErC and pmErC following a protocol developed by Yeung et al., 2017, which is derived from a functional connectivity study (Maass et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROI definition method with citations.

claims.claim: The mean within-subject correlation for perceived similarity ratings across two sessions was 0.84.
claims.source: The mean within-subject correlation across the two sessions was 0.84, indicating high stability of participant's perceived similarity ratings over 1 week.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by test-retest data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Intrasubject correlations were significantly higher than intersubject correlations for perceived similarity ratings.
claims.source: Critically, a paired t-test (intrasubject > intersubject correlation) confirmed that intrasubject correlations were significantly higher than intersubject correlations (p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The perceived similarity structure that is unique to the individual observer is a stable characteristic.
claims.source: This pattern of results indicates that the perceived similarity structure that is unique to the individual observer is a stable characteristic.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of intrasubject versus intersubject correlations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Intersubject correlations were reduced for high similarity exemplars compared to low similarity exemplars.
claims.source: There are also hints that this variability is most pronounced at the finest grain of judgements, as reflected in reduced intersubject correlations for high similarity exemplars (high r = 0.64; medium r = 0.65, low r = 0.72; high < low; t(22) = 3.41; p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of intersubject correlations at different levels of similarity.

claims.claim: Stability of activity patterns was significant for all regions and did not interact with level of similarity.
claims.source: This pattern of results cannot be attributed to differences in stability of activity patterns across levels of similarity for different regions; supplementary analyses revealed that stability was significant for all regions and did not interact with level of similarity (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Patterns in LOC are distinguishable only at lowest level of perceived similarity within categories.
claims.source: Results from one tailed t-tests to probe whether classifier performance was above chance indicate that patterns in LOC are distinguishable only at lowest level of perceived similarity within categories.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: PrC and alErC are only regions in which patterns are distinguishable at medium and high levels of perceived similarity.
claims.source: PrC and alErC are only regions in which patterns are distinguishable at medium and high levels of perceived similarity (*p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Patterns in all ROIs show stable similarity structure as reflected in significant correlations between odd and even runs.
claims.source: Patterns in all region of interests (ROIs) show stable similarity structure as reflected in significant correlations between odd and even run; ***p < 0.001, Bonferroni-corrected based on regions; error bars represent standard error of the mean (SEM).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by split-half reliability analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Patterns in all ROIs are unique to each individual as reflected in significant brain–brain i-index.
claims.source: Patterns in all ROIs are unique to each individual as reflected in significant brain–brain i-index (i.e., within minus between subject correlation; ***p < 0.001, Bonferroni-corrected based on regions, with testing against a null distribution created by randomizing subject labels; error bars represent SEM estimated based on randomization).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by brain-brain i-index analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Research that has aimed to characterize the nature of object representations in human PrC with fMRI has shown that the degree of feature overlap between objects is captured by activation patterns in this region.
claims.source: Research that has aimed to characterize the nature of object representations in human PrC with fMRI has shown that the degree of feature overlap between objects is captured by activation patterns in this region. Such a relationship has been revealed in multiple task contexts, with images of real-world objects and with words denoting such objects; moreover, it has been observed for feature overlap at the perceptual as well as the semantic level (Clarke and Tyler, 2014; Erez et al., 2016; Bruffaerts et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies on PrC.

claims.claim: Findings from lesion studies support the idea that medial temporal lobe structures downstream from IT play a critical role in processes required for the appreciation of fine-grained visual similarities between complex real-world objects.
claims.source: Findings from lesion studies conducted with oddity-discrimination tasks support the idea that medial temporal lobe structures downstream from IT play a critical role in processes required for the appreciation of fine-grained visual similarities between complex real-world objects that are expressed in perceptual reports (see Bonnen et al., 2021, for review).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of lesion studies.

claims.claim: Barense et al., 2007 found that individuals with medial temporal lobe lesions including PrC and ErC showed impairments in identifying the odd-one out item in sets of images of real-world objects that shared a high number of overlapping visual features.
claims.source: For example, Barense et al., 2007 compared performance on multiple visual oddity tasks between individuals with lesions in the medial temporal lobe that largely spared PrC and ErC, versus individuals with more widespread damage in the medial temporal lobes that included PrC and ErC. Most notably, individuals in the latter but not in the former group showed impairments in identifying the odd-one out item in sets of images of real-world objects that shared a high number of overlapping visual features.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific lesion study.

claims.claim: The anatomical specificity of fMRI findings in the medial temporal lobe is striking, with activity patterns reflecting similarity structure present in PrC and alErC but absent in pmErC and PhC.
claims.source: The anatomical specificity of our fMRI findings in the medial temporal lobe is striking. While activity patterns that reflected the similarity structure among category exemplars were present in PrC and alErC, they were absent in medial temporal regions that have previously been implicated in visual discrimination of scenes, specifically pmErC and PhC cortex (see Schultz et al., 2015, for review).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the pattern of RSA results across different MTL regions and citation to prior research.

claims.claim: PrC is connected to alErC, and PhC is connected to pmErC, reflecting differences in functional connectivity related to object versus scene processing.
claims.source: This specificity is noteworthy in light of documented differences in functional connectivity between these regions that have been linked to object versus scene processing, with PrC being connected to alErC, and PhC being connected to pmErC, respectively (Maass et al., 2015; see Schröder et al., 2015 for more broadly distributed differences in functional connectivity between ErC subregions and other cortical structures).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional connectivity studies.

claims.claim: The component of perceived similarity structure that was shared by observers showed a statistical relationship to the estimates of the HMAX model.
claims.source: Notably, the component of perceived similarity structure that was shared by observers showed a statistical relationship to the estimates of the HMAX model, which describes objects at the intermediate feature level and which has been linked to LOC representations in prior work (Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Cadieu et al., 2007; Serre et al., 2007; but see Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014, Kubilius et al., 2016 for limitations as compared to deep convolutional neural network models).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses and citations to prior work on HMAX.

claims.claim: The fine-grained similarity structure among exemplars that led to the largest number of confusion errors in behavioural discrimination was predominantly observer specific.
claims.source: The fine-grained similarity structure among exemplars that led to the largest number of confusion errors in behavioural discrimination on the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task during scanning was predominantly observer specific, and this fine-grained observer-specific structure was solely predicted by activity patterns in PrC and alErC.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of behavioral and fMRI results at high levels of similarity.

claims.claim: The coding of objects in PrC and alErC as fully integrated entities based on complex feature conjunctions affords the flexibility required to capture fine-grained differentiation among exemplars that characterizes the perception of individual observers.
claims.source: The coding of objects in PrC and alErC as fully integrated entities based on complex feature conjunctions arguably affords the flexibility that is required to capture the fine-grained differentiation among exemplars that characterizes the perception of individual observers.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings based on the representational-hierarchical model.

claims.claim: Charest et al., 2014 revealed observer-specific effects in the similarity structure of activity patterns in IT that were tied to participants' reports for highly familiar real-world objects with unique personal meaning.
claims.source: Charest et al., 2014 revealed observer-specific effects in the similarity structure of activity patterns in IT that were tied to participants' reports for highly familiar real-world objects with unique personal meaning (e.g., images of observers' own car, their own bicycle).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study.

claims.claim: Collins and Behrmann, 2020 showed that just a few days of repeated exposure can lead to increased differentiation among exemplars, with changes most pronounced at the level of fine-grained similarity structure when observers have had some prior experience with the category.

results.result: Perceived visual similarity among category exemplars shows both shared and observer-specific components. The mean intersubject correlation was r=0.69, and average ratings correlated with HMAX model estimates (r=0.25) only at low and medium similarity levels. Individual differences in perceived similarity are temporally stable (within-subject r=0.84 across sessions), with intrasubject correlations significantly higher than intersubject correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17, C45-C48 provide converging behavioral evidence from the iMDS task showing both shared structure (correlation with HMAX) and observer-specific structure (test-retest reliability, intra>inter-subject correlations). The statistical tests are appropriate and the pattern is internally consistent across multiple analyses.

results.result: Behavioral discrimination performance during the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task was highly sensitive to perceived visual similarity among exemplars. Error rates and response times increased with increasing similarity, and performance was more sensitive to participants' own similarity ratings than to other participants' ratings.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C18-C20 demonstrate clear behavioral effects with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests with significant p-values). The finding that own ratings predict performance better than others' ratings (C20) provides strong evidence for observer-specific effects in behavior, supported by Figure 2B,C.

results.result: Activity patterns in PrC and alErC, as well as EVC and LOC, significantly correlated with participants' perceived visual similarity RDMs. However, patterns in scene-processing regions (PhC and pmErC) did not predict perceived similarity structure for objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C12, C21-C23 are supported by ROI-based RSA results shown in Figure 3D with appropriate Bonferroni correction. The anatomical specificity (significant in object regions, not scene regions) strengthens the interpretation. Statistical thresholds are clearly reported.

results.result: PrC and alErC activity patterns predicted perceived similarity at all three levels (low, medium, high), while posterior VVS regions (EVC, LOC) only predicted similarity at the lowest level. Classification analyses confirmed that exemplar patterns are distinguishable in PrC/alErC at medium and high similarity levels but only at low levels in LOC. Whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed PrC and alErC as the only regions predicting high-level similarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28, C49-C51 provide converging evidence from multiple analysis approaches (level-specific RSA, classification, searchlight) all pointing to superior fine-grained discrimination in PrC/alErC. The control analysis (C49) rules out differential stability as an alternative explanation. Results are supported by Figures 4 and 5 with appropriate corrections.

results.result: Activity patterns in posterior VVS regions (EVC, LOC) correlated with HMAX model estimates and average similarity ratings at low and medium levels, but PrC and alErC did not correlate with HMAX or average ratings at any level. This suggests posterior regions capture shared, intermediate-feature-level similarity while PrC/alErC represent more integrated object representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C59 are supported by RSA analyses comparing brain patterns to HMAX estimates (Figure 6). The dissociation between posterior regions (correlate with HMAX) and PrC/alErC (do not correlate) is clear and statistically significant with appropriate corrections. The interpretation (C31) follows logically from the data pattern.

results.result: Neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC uniquely predict observer-specific perceived visual similarity structure, including at high levels of similarity. Posterior VVS regions (EVC, LOC) did not show this observer-specific mapping. All ROIs showed unique individual patterns (brain-brain i-index), but only PrC/alErC patterns predicted individual behavioral reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34, C53, C60 are supported by i-index analyses (Figure 7) showing within-subject correlations significantly exceed between-subject correlations for PrC/alErC but not posterior regions. The control analysis (C53) confirms individual patterns exist everywhere, but only PrC/alErC patterns map to individual perceptual reports. Statistical tests with appropriate corrections are provided.

results.result: The study included 29 participants initially, with 23 included in final analyses after exclusions for head motion, behavioral performance, and signal quality. All participants were right-handed, fluent in English, with no psychiatric or neurological disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C68 provide clear methodological details about the sample. Exclusion criteria are reasonable and clearly specified (motion >0.8mm, performance >2SD below mean, tSNR >2SD below mean). Final n=23 is adequate for fMRI studies with within-subject designs.

results.result: The study used 40 greyscale images from 10 categories (4 exemplars per category) selected from the Migo Normative Database with varying levels of perceived visual similarity. Stimuli were validated in a pilot study (n=40) to ensure similarity ratings matched normative values.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C69-C70 describe stimulus selection and validation. The use of a normative database and pilot validation strengthens stimulus selection. The structure (10 categories × 4 exemplars) is appropriate for the experimental design.

results.result: The Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task involved 8 runs of 4 minutes each, with each exemplar presented 24 times on no-response trials across the experiment. Only no-response trials were analyzed to avoid motor confounds, ensuring no analyzed trials were immediate neighbors. Participants practiced before scanning with different stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40, C77-C80 describe the experimental design with appropriate detail. The decision to analyze only no-response trials (C78) is methodologically sound to avoid motor confounds. The inference that analyzed trials were not neighbors (C79) follows logically from the design. Practice with different stimuli (C80) is good experimental practice.

results.result: fMRI data were acquired at 3T with ultra-high resolution (1.7×1.7mm in-plane) to optimize differentiation of BOLD signal in alErC versus pmErC. Acquisition included MP-RAGE (0.8mm isotropic), T2-weighted imaging, and functional runs with 42 slices acquired in odd-even interleaved fashion. Total scan time was approximately 60 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C81-C84 provide comprehensive MRI acquisition parameters. The rationale for ultra-high resolution (C42) is clearly stated and appropriate for distinguishing MTL subregions. All technical parameters are specified in sufficient detail for replication.

results.result: ROIs were defined using multiple methods: automated segmentation (ASHS) for PrC, ErC, PhC; manual segmentation of ErC into alErC/pmErC following Yeung et al. 2017 protocol; probabilistic atlases for EVC and TP; and functional localizer for LOC (intact>scrambled objects, p<0.01 uncorrected).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C90-C91 describe ROI definition methods with appropriate citations. The combination of automated, manual, atlas-based, and functional approaches is methodologically sound. The manual segmentation protocol for ErC subregions (C44) is based on established methods. The functional localizer threshold for LOC (C91) is standard but uncorrected, which is typical for ROI definition.

results.result: Preprocessing used fmriprep-v1.1.8 including motion correction, slice-time correction, distortion correction, and CompCor-based noise correction. First-level analyses were conducted in native space without smoothing to preserve high-resolution patterns. RSA used Pearson correlations between exemplar-specific patterns. Searchlight analysis used 100-voxel neighborhoods with TFCE correction (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89, C92-C94 describe preprocessing and analysis methods with appropriate detail and citations. The use of fmriprep (C85) is standard practice. CompCor noise correction (C87) is appropriate for high-resolution fMRI. No smoothing (C88) is justified for MVPA. TFCE correction (C94) is appropriate for searchlight analyses.

results.result: Behavioral similarity data were processed using a MATLAB toolbox to calculate pairwise distances and convert to dissimilarity percentiles. Levels were defined to be non-overlapping (≥0.1 percentile separation), and the range of dissimilarity percentiles did not differ significantly between levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 describe behavioral data processing with appropriate methods. The criterion for non-overlapping levels (C73) is reasonable. The verification that ranges don't differ between levels (C74) is an important control, though the statistical test used is not specified.

results.result: Activity patterns in all ROIs showed stable similarity structure as reflected in significant correlations between odd and even runs (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected).
results.evaluation: Claim C52 reports split-half reliability across all ROIs with appropriate statistical correction. This is an important control analysis demonstrating data quality. Results are shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

results.result: The manuscript situates the current work within established knowledge about visual object processing, the representational-hierarchical model, and prior fMRI and lesion studies. This includes general statements about the field, theoretical frameworks, and citations to relevant prior work on PrC/ErC function, HMAX model properties, and learning-related plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C3-C10, C54-C58, C62-C64, C66, C75-C76 provide appropriate context through citations to prior work. These are primarily background claims supported by citations rather than new empirical findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent prior work, though detailed verification of each citation is beyond the scope of this review.

results.result: The authors interpret their findings within the representational-hierarchical framework, suggesting that complex feature conjunctions in PrC/alErC afford flexibility to capture observer-specific fine-grained differentiation. They speculate this may reflect individual differences in perceptual expertise and emphasize the value of studying subjective similarity and observer variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C65, C67 are interpretive and speculative statements about mechanisms and implications. While these interpretations are reasonable given the data, they go beyond what is directly demonstrated. C61 and C65 are explicitly speculative ("arguably," "may reflect"). C67 is a concluding statement about research implications rather than an empirical claim. These are appropriate for a Discussion section but cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported empirical results.
